entities.name: Acacius of Sebaste
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Acacius of Sebaste (died c. 251) was a Christian priest and martyr who died during the Decian Persecution under Emperor Decius, one of the most systematic Roman campaigns against Christianity. He served as a priest in Sebaste (modern Sivas in Turkey), where a community of Christian soldiers — the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste — had already been executed for their faith under Emperor Licinius in 320. Acacius is distinct from this earlier group but associated with Sebaste's tradition of Christian martyrdom.

The Decian Persecution (249–251) required all Roman citizens to sacrifice to the Roman gods and obtain a certificate (libellus) of compliance. Christians who refused faced imprisonment, torture, and execution. Acacius's refusal to sacrifice placed him within the pattern of clerical martyrdom that shaped the Church's identity as a community capable of producing witnesses unto death.

His veneration in both the Roman and Byzantine traditions reflects the early Church's dual heritage of Latin and Greek martyrology. The city of Sebaste had multiple layers of Christian martyrdom associated with it — including the Forty Soldiers — giving it exceptional significance in early Christian holy geography. Acacius's feast day is celebrated in both traditions.
